I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding

- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.

- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy

- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Economic Census
Description: The Economic Census is the official five-year measure of businesses in the United States providing comprehensive statistics at the national, state, and local levels. It serves as the benchmark for current economic activity, such as the Gross Domestic Product and Producer Price Index.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Economic Census comprehensively. Let me start with some web searches to verify and supplement my knowledge.The description checks out. Let me research the history, users, and data access/preservation aspects in more depth.I now have comprehensive, verified information. Here is the full report.

---

# Research Report: The Economic Census (United States)

## 1. Verification of the Description You Provided

Your description is **accurate**. It matches, nearly word-for-word, the U.S. Census Bureau's own official language:

> "The Economic Census is the official five-year measure of businesses in the United States providing comprehensive statistics at the national, state, and local levels. It serves as the benchmark for current economic activity, such as the Gross Domestic Product and Producer Price Index." — census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census.html

One nuance worth adding: the Census Bureau's fuller description also notes that the Economic Census provides "information on business locations, the workforce, and trillions of dollars of sales by product and service type," and that it covers "most industries and geographic areas of the United States and Island Areas" (Puerto Rico, Guam, American Samoa, U.S. Virgin Islands, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands).

---

## 2. Publisher and Administration

- **Publishing agency:** U.S. Census Bureau, an agency of the **U.S. Department of Commerce**.
- **Cadence:** Conducted every five years, for reference years ending in **"2" and "7"** (e.g., 2017, 2022; the 2027 Economic Census is next). Data are collected in the year following the reference year.
- **Statistical framework:** Data are classified using the **North American Industry Classification System (NAICS)** and product detail using the **North American Product Classification System (NAPCS)** — both jointly maintained with Canada and Mexico, which matters for cross-national comparability.
- **Scale (2022 cycle):** Approximately 950 detailed industries across 19 sectors; tables for nearly 21,000 geographic areas (nation, states, metro areas, counties, economic places, and ZIP codes); over 7,900 goods and services products.

---

## 3. Legal Authority and Mandate

This is one of the most important aspects for preservationists and policy activists: the Economic Census is **not discretionary** — it is required by statute.

- **Title 13, U.S. Code, Section 131** mandates that the Secretary of Commerce "take, compile, and publish censuses of manufactures, of mineral industries, and of other businesses, including the distributive trades, service establishments, and transportation... every fifth year." (Codified 1954; amended by P.L. 85-207 (1957) and P.L. 88-532 (1964).)
- **Title 13, Sections 182, 191, 224, and 225** authorize the collection, make response **mandatory** for sampled businesses, and specify penalties for non-response.
- **Title 13, Section 9** provides the confidentiality guarantee: individual responses may be seen only by sworn Census Bureau employees, used only for statistical purposes, and copies retained by respondents are immune from legal process. Responses are also exempt from Freedom of Information Act disclosure.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act:** Each cycle goes through OMB review with Federal Register notices (e.g., the August 4, 2015 notice for the 2017 census), which document respondent burden — useful records for researchers studying the administrative history of the dataset.

**Policy implication:** Because the census is statutorily mandated, defunding or degrading it requires either congressional appropriations choices or statutory change — both of which are matters of public record and advocacy targets. The mandatory-response nature also means any shift to voluntary response (as has happened in some other countries' business censuses) would fundamentally change data quality.

---

## 4. History

The Economic Census has one of the longest pedigrees of any federal dataset — over two centuries:

| Period | Development |
|---|---|
| **1810** | First census of manufactures, taken alongside the decennial population census by federal marshals, under a May 1, 1810 act of Congress (prompted by Treasury Secretary Albert Gallatin's complaint that he lacked statistical data to make policy recommendations on manufacturing). Covered 25 broad categories of manufactured products and 200+ kinds of goods. |
| **1840** | Questions added on mining and some commercial activities. |
| **1902–1905** | Congress creates the permanent Census Bureau (1902) and directs a quinquennial census of manufactures. The **1905 Census of Manufactures** was the first census of any kind taken separately from the decennial census, and the first conducted largely by mail. |
| **1921–1939** | Biennial censuses of manufactures. |
| **1930** | First Census of Business, covering retail and wholesale trade; construction industries added; broadened to some service trades in 1933. |
| **WWII** | Economic censuses suspended in favor of war-oriented surveys. Resumed with the 1947 Census of Manufactures and 1948 Census of Business. |
| **1954** | First fully integrated economic census — consistent concepts, definitions, classifications, and reporting units across sectors. First use of an electronic computer (UNIVAC I) for processing. |
| **1963** | Administrative records (IRS/SSA data) begin substituting for questionnaires for very small firms. |
| **1967** | Current "years ending in 2 and 7" schedule established; construction census begins on a regular basis. |
| **1997** | Major classification shift from the Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) to **NAICS** — a critical break in the time series that all longitudinal users must account for. |
| **2012–2022** | Transition to electronic/online response (the 2012 census was the first conducted almost entirely electronically); data dissemination moves to data.census.gov and APIs. |

**For preservationists:** Historical volumes exist in print and PDF going back to the 19th century; the Census Bureau maintains an "Economic Census History" page and historical working papers (e.g., "Historical Development of the Economic Census in the United States" and "The Censuses of Manufactures: 1810–1890"). The Library of Congress and Federal Depository Library Program hold legacy publications. Original 1810–era manufacturing schedules are in National Archives Record Group 29.

---

## 5. Methodology and Scope (What Data Scientists Need to Know)

**Frame and collection:**
- Establishments are selected from the Census Bureau's **Business Register**, built from prior censuses/surveys plus IRS and SSA administrative records, supplemented by Bureau of Labor Statistics industry classifications.
- Large and multi-unit companies receive questionnaires; most small single-unit firms are **not** canvassed — their data are imputed from administrative records (a key caveat for interpreting "census" completeness).
- 2022 timeline: classification requests to small businesses began October 24, 2022; main mailing January 31, 2023; responses due March 15, 2023.

**Core statistics:** number of establishments; sales/value of shipments/revenue; employment; payroll; plus industry-specific items and product-line detail (NAPCS).

**Coverage limitations:**
- Excludes most of agriculture (covered by the USDA Census of Agriculture), rail transportation (covered by regulators), private households, and most of public administration/government (covered by the Census of Governments). The 2022 cycle added selected support activities for agriculture and forestry (NAICS 115).
- The 1997 SIC→NAICS transition breaks comparability; even between 2017 and 2022, NAICS revisions required special "Bridge" tables.

**Disclosure avoidance:**
- **Cell suppression** (primary and complementary): cells that could reveal an individual business's data are replaced with "D"; additional cells suppressed so values can't be derived by subtraction.
- **Noise infusion** is also used for business data as an alternative to suppression.
- Rows with fewer than three contributing firms/establishments are not published.
- Higher-level totals are generally unaffected by suppression, but non-published cells and derived values "are not official and may differ substantially from the true estimate."

---

## 6. Data Products and Access

**2022 release schedule (flow basis, January 2024 – March 2026):**
1. **First Look Statistics** (Jan 2024) — preliminary U.S.-level data at 2–3 digit NAICS
2. **Geographic Area Statistics** (Dec 2024) — the flagship release: all sectors and geographies simultaneously (a change from prior flow releases)
3. **Comparative & Bridge Statistics** (Feb 2025) — 2022 vs. 2017, including NAICS-change bridges
4. **Establishment and Firm Size Statistics** (Apr 2025) — size distributions, concentration ratios, legal form of organization
5. **Product Statistics** (May 2025) — NAPCS-based
6. **Miscellaneous/Industry-Specific Statistics** (Dec 2024 – Apr 2026)
7. **Island Area Statistics** (June–Dec 2024)

**Access channels:**
- **data.census.gov** — formatted tables, customizable, downloadable as XLS/CSV/ZIP (2012, 2017, 2022)
- **Census API** — Economic Census data available programmatically from 2002 forward (census.gov/data/developers)
- **FTP files** — for tables too large for data.census.gov
- **Legacy formats** — older censuses (pre-2012) via American FactFinder archives, CD-ROM/DVD, and print; preservationists should note that American FactFinder was retired in 2020, creating known access gaps for pre-2012 tabular data
- **Microdata access:** Confidential establishment-level microdata are available to researchers with approved projects and Special Sworn Status through the **Federal Statistical Research Data Centers (FSRDCs)** — the source of much influential economics research (e.g., on firm dynamics, productivity, and market concentration)

**Related/derived programs** (important context — these depend on the Economic Census): County Business Patterns, Survey of Business Owners, Commodity Flow Survey, Business Dynamics Statistics, and the benchmarking of virtually all Census economic surveys.

---

## 7. Typical Users and Uses

**Federal statistical system (arguably the most consequential use):**
- Benchmarks the **GDP** accounts (Bureau of Economic Analysis), **Producer Price Index** (BLS), and Federal Reserve industrial production indexes
- Provides sampling frames and benchmark totals for the Census Bureau's own monthly, quarterly, and annual economic surveys — without the Economic Census, the entire "current economic indicators" ecosystem drifts

**State and local governments:** economic development planning, fiscal forecasting, incentive targeting, understanding local industry composition at county/place/ZIP level — the Economic Census is the *only* source of detailed industry data for small geographies.

**Businesses and private sector:** site selection, market sizing, competitive analysis, sales territory planning, capital investment decisions. Trade associations and chambers of commerce use it for member benchmarking.

**Researchers and academics:** industrial organization, labor economics, urban economics, entrepreneurship research (especially via FSRDC microdata); market concentration studies have relied heavily on the concentration-ratio tables.

**Journalists and policy advocates:** documenting industry concentration, small-business ecosystems, regional economic change, and the geography of economic opportunity.

---

## 8. Benefits to the Public

1. **Foundational infrastructure:** It is the statistical "benchmark" that makes nearly every other U.S. economic indicator trustworthy. GDP revisions in benchmark years are anchored to Economic Census data.
2. **Geographic equity:** No private data provider replicates comprehensive industry data down to the county, place, and ZIP-code level — small towns and rural areas are visible in this data in a way they are nowhere else.
3. **Free and public:** All tabular products are free online, supporting small businesses and community organizations that could never afford commercial market data.
4. **Evidence-based policy:** Enables policymakers at all levels to target economic development, disaster recovery (e.g., post-disaster business recovery analyses), and workforce investment.
5. **Confidentiality with utility:** The Title 13 framework achieves unusually high response rates (mandatory response plus strong legal confidentiality), producing data quality that voluntary surveys cannot match.
6. **Historical continuity:** A 200+ year time series of the American economy, from blacksmithing to robotics.

---

## 9. Issues and Concerns for Preservationists, Librarians, and Advocates

- **Platform churn:** The retirement of American FactFinder (2020) and migration to data.census.gov broke links and changed access patterns for pre-2012 data. Data librarians should verify local copies or archived snapshots of legacy tables; the Internet Archive and depository libraries hold important legacy formats.
- **Long release lag:** Data for reference year 2022 were not fully released until March 2026 — a 3+ year lag inherent to the scale of the operation, and a perennial target of criticism and budget trade-offs.
- **Classification instability:** SIC→NAICS (1997) and quinquennial NAICS revisions complicate longitudinal analysis; the Bridge tables are essential but imperfect.
- **Suppression and small-area data gaps:** Disclosure avoidance means many detailed industry × small-geography cells are unavailable — a real limitation for rural economic research.
- **Funding vulnerability:** Although statutorily mandated, adequacy of appropriations is a live political issue. Census Bureau budget pressures in the 2020s have raised concerns among data users about the scope and timeliness of the 2027 cycle — an area where policy activism (e.g., via the Census Project coalition and American Statistical Association) has historically mattered.
- **Non-sampled small firms:** The growing reliance on administrative records for small firms is efficient but means data quality for that segment depends on IRS/SSA data-sharing arrangements, which themselves can be politically fragile.
- **Digital preservation:** Tables on data.census.gov are not guaranteed permanent URLs; preservationists should capture the FTP bulk files and table IDs (e.g., EC2200-series) for each release, plus methodology and technical documentation pages.

---

## 10. Key Sources for Further Research

- census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census.html (program home)
- 2022 Economic Census: census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022.html (methodology, release schedule, FAQ)
- 13 U.S.C. §131 (statutory mandate); §§9, 182, 191, 224, 225
- Census Bureau, "Economic Census History" and the working paper "Historical Development of the Economic Census in the United States"
- Bohme, Frederick G., "U.S. economic censuses, 1810 to the present," *Government Information Quarterly* 4(3), 1987
- Library of Congress Research Guide: "Economic Census – U.S. Census Connections"
- Census API documentation: census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/economic-census.2022.html
- FSRDC program (microdata access): census.gov/fsrdc

---

**Bottom line:** The Economic Census is a statutorily mandated (Title 13 U.S.C. §131), quinquennial, mandatory-response census of U.S. business conducted by the Census Bureau, with roots in 1810 and continuous quinquennial operation since 1967. It is the benchmark for GDP, the PPI, and the entire federal economic statistical system; the only source of detailed industry data for small geographies; and a public good used by governments, businesses, researchers, and communities — while carrying real challenges around release lag, classification changes, disclosure-related suppression, platform migration, and funding adequacy that preservationists and advocates should monitor.

I'll research current conditions affecting the Census Bureau and the Economic Census — staffing, funding, FY2026 budget proposals, the 2027 Economic Census cycle, and any administration-driven changes.Now let me check the 2027 Economic Census planning status, Federal Register ICR notices, and historical data availability.Two more checks: the 2027 Economic Census planning status and Census Bureau leadership changes.# Risk Assessment: U.S. Economic Census (Census Bureau, Department of Commerce)

**Assessment date context:** Research current through mid-2026 (FY2026 appropriations enacted as P.L. 119-74; 2022 Economic Census release cycle completed March 2026; 2027 Economic Census collection planned for calendar 2028).

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence gathered:**

- **Supporting "No Known Issue":** The Census Bureau's "Economic Census Data Tables and FTP Files by Year" page confirms 2012, 2017, and 2022 formatted tables remain live on data.census.gov with full download options (XLS/CSV/ZIP); 2002 and 2007 remain available as FTP files; pre-2002 data remain available as official print/PDF publications in the Census Library. The bureau explicitly states that ZIP code tables "released for previous economic censuses will remain accessible to data users" (most recent: 2012). No reports of removal or alteration of any prior-cycle Economic Census files since January 2025. The 2022 Comparative and Bridge tables were *reissued* (April 24, 2025) with an enhanced suppression pattern — a documented, transparent correction with a public errata note, not a silent alteration.
- **Supporting "High Risk":** None found — no prior-year files removed.
- **Supporting "Moderate Risk":** The only data *element* loss — ZIP code geography — was discontinued beginning with the 2017 cycle (a pre-2025 decision), and prior ZIP tables remain online. The discontinuation of the American FactFinder platform (2020) reduced convenience of access to pre-2012 tabular data but FTP/print surrogates persist.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** All prior-cycle files remain accessible; corrections have been transparent and versioned. Preservationists should still mirror the FTP bulk files given platform churn risk, but no actual removal has occurred.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence gathered:**

- **Supporting "No Known Issue":** The 2022 Economic Census completed its full release schedule on time (First Look, January 2024; all releases complete by March 2026, as promised). A Federal Register notice (91 FR 56835, "Current Mandatory Business Surveys," 2026) explicitly confirms: "The next Economic Census will occur in 2028 for the reference year 2027." The FY2026 budget justification includes continued Economic Census activities.
- **Supporting "Moderate Risk":** The OMB clearance for the Economic Census (Control No. 0607-0998, "2022 Economic Census (Stateside and Island Areas)") **expired June 30, 2025**, and as of the latest available reginfo.gov/omb.report inventory (filings through July 2026), no reinstatement ICR for the 2027 cycle has yet been filed — i.e., the ICR has been expired up to one year. Mitigating context: this is partly an artifact of the quinquennial cycle (clearances lapse between cycles; the analogous 2022-cycle reinstatement FRN was published ~16 months before collection, which would correspond to roughly late summer 2026 for the 2027 census). A lapse stretching past late 2026 without a 60-day Federal Register notice would escalate this to a genuine schedule risk.
- **Supporting "High Risk":** Not currently met — no statutory deadline missed (collection isn't due until 2028), and the lapse has not yet exceeded one year.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** Publication of the 2022 cycle was fully on time, and the next collection is officially confirmed — but the controlling ICR has been expired for roughly a year with no renewal filed yet, which matches the rubric's Moderate definition ("ICR expired up to one year"). This should be re-checked when the expected 2027-cycle 60-day FRN window (mid-to-late 2026) passes.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence gathered:**

- **Supporting "No Known Issue":** The 2022 cycle delivered its complete planned product suite — Geographic Area, Comparative, Bridge, Establishment/Firm Size, Product (NAPCS), Miscellaneous, and Island Area statistics — on the published schedule, with no reductions in granularity, frequency, or scope versus the 2017 cycle. The Bridge tables were actually *moved up* in the schedule "to better serve data user needs."
- **Supporting "Moderate Risk":** Multiple credible emerging risks: (a) the Census Bureau has lost an estimated **15% of staff since FY2024** (American Statistical Association, "The Nation's Data at Risk 2025"); (b) the FY2026 President's Budget proposed cutting the **Periodic Economic Statistics account — which contains the Economic Census — by $18 million (~11%)** (from $162M to $144M); (c) government-wide hiring freezes and a Commerce Department requirement that the Secretary personally approve contracts over $100,000 created a backlog of 3,000+ requests, disrupting survey operations; (d) a Commerce inspector general evaluation found the bureau lacks effective strategies for staffing gaps and high field-representative vacancies; (e) AP reported data-product cancellations elsewhere in the statistical system amid these pressures. None of these has yet degraded Economic Census output, but they directly threaten the 2027 planning runway.
- **Supporting "High Risk":** Not met — no actual reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency have occurred in the current cycle. (The ZIP-code granularity loss dates to 2017, predating this assessment window.)

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** Current output is intact and on time, but staffing attrition, a proposed double-digit cut to the very account funding the census, and documented operational backlogs constitute a textbook "potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency" — particularly for the 2027 cycle now entering planning.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence gathered:**

- **Supporting "No Known Issue":** The Economic Census is among the most strongly statutorily anchored datasets in the federal system. **13 U.S.C. §131** explicitly requires the Secretary of Commerce to "take, compile, and publish" these business censuses every five years; §§182, 191, 224–225 govern scope, mandatory response, and enforcement; §9 guarantees confidentiality. The OMB ICR itself names the authorizing statutes (13 U.S.C. 131, 191, 193). There is **no substitute collection**: it is the only source of detailed industry data for small geographies, and it is the legally embedded benchmark for GDP (BEA), the PPI (BLS), and the sampling frames of every Census current economic survey — the Annual Integrated Economic Survey notice itself describes the current surveys as existing "for the period between economic censuses." Notably, the FY2026 budget's language about eliminating functions "not statutorily mandated" implicitly *protects* the Economic Census.
- **Supporting "Moderate"/"High":** None applicable.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** Explicit statutory mandate, named authorization, no alternatives, and direct requirement for implementation of core federal economic programs (national accounts).

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence gathered:**

- **Supporting "High Risk":** Per the rubric's explicit thresholds: (a) **1,000+ staff lost** — AFGE Council 241 reports approximately **1,300–1,500 Census Bureau employees** lost since January 2025 via deferred resignation, voluntary separation, and early retirement, plus ~100 RIF notices at the Tucson call center during the October 2025 shutdown; (b) **leadership removed** — Director Robert Santos resigned in February 2025, roughly two years before his term's end, leaving the bureau under acting leadership; at least five division/office chiefs (including two working on 2030 census preparations) departed, and vacancies emerged on the Data Stewardship Executive Policy Committee that safeguards confidentiality decisions; (c) the ASA estimates a **15% workforce decline since FY24**, with the FY2026 request seeking a further 9% overall staffing reduction and a 27% cut to periodic-censuses staffing.
- **Supporting "Moderate Risk":** On budget: the **enacted** FY2026 CJS bill (P.L. 119-74) provides **$1.49 billion — an increase of ~$108M (~8%) over FY2024/FY2025** — so there is no enacted bureau-wide budget cut. However, the FY2026 *request* cut Current Surveys and Programs ~12% and Periodic Economic Statistics ~11% ($18M), and House Democrats' summary confirms Current Surveys and Programs were cut $30M below FY2025 in the enacted bill. Staffing loss percentage (~15–18%) falls in the 10–39% Moderate band.
- **Supporting "No Known Issue":** Clearly not met.

**Selected level: High Risk.** Although the percentage loss (~15–18%) is in the Moderate band and the topline budget rose, the rubric's High threshold is triggered on two independent criteria: **1,000+ staff lost** (met: ~1,300–1,500) and **leadership removed** (met: the director's premature resignation plus five division chiefs). A mitigating note for fairness: the losses are bureau-wide and concentrated in decennial/demographic programs and field operations; the economic directorate has not been specifically targeted, which is why the effects have not yet shown up in category 3.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence gathered:**

- **Supporting "Moderate Risk":** Several proposed/pending changes and official statements bear on Census economic programs: (a) the FY2026 budget "supports the President's Budget proposal to **reorganize BLS, BEA, and the Census Bureau at the Department of Commerce**" — an unresolved, significant structural change; (b) the budget directs the bureau to eliminate functions "not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" by end of FY2026 (the EC itself is statutorily mandated, but its supporting programs may not all be); (c) **DOGE announced termination of five Census-conducted surveys** ($16.5M, conducted for other agencies) and stated other surveys are being reviewed "one-by-one"; (d) the House FY2026 CJS bill proposed Section 605, which would have capped all Census surveys at two follow-up inquiries — devastating to response rates for a mandatory establishment census — though it was **excluded from the final enacted bill**; (e) the administration's broader posture toward economic statistics (e.g., the August 2025 firing of the BLS commissioner) signals willingness to intervene in economic data agencies.
- **Supporting "No Known Issue":** For the Economic Census specifically, no changes to content, scope, or publication have been made since January 2025; no Presidential-Action-driven ICR affects it; no negative policy note appears on its pages.
- **Supporting "High Risk":** Not met — nothing has actually been changed or terminated for this dataset.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** The dataset itself is untouched, but there are multiple live, documented proposals and administration statements — a proposed tri-agency reorganization, program-elimination directives, and an ongoing one-by-one DOGE review of Census surveys — that squarely match "proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned."

---

## Summary

| Category | Risk Level | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Data Availability | **No Known Issue** | All prior cycles (2012–2022 online; 2002/2007 FTP; pre-2002 print/PDF) remain accessible; corrections transparent |
| Future Data Availability | **Moderate Risk** | 2022 cycle completed on time and 2027 collection officially confirmed, but ICR 0607-0998 expired 6/30/2025 with renewal not yet filed |
| Data Quality | **Moderate Risk** | Output intact to date; emerging risk from 15% staffing loss, proposed 11% cut to Periodic Economic Statistics, contract backlogs |
| Statutory Context | **No Known Issue** | Explicitly mandated by 13 U.S.C. §131; no substitutes; required for GDP/PPI benchmarking |
| Staffing and Funding | **High Risk** | ~1,300–1,500 staff lost (>1,000 threshold); director resigned prematurely; five division chiefs departed — despite an 8% topline FY2026 budget increase |
| Policy | **Moderate Risk** | Proposed Census/BLS/BEA reorganization, "non-mandated functions" elimination directive, DOGE survey-by-survey review; no changes yet made to this dataset |

**Overall interpretation:** The Economic Census is in the strongest possible legal position (explicit Title 13 mandate, no substitutes) and its data holdings and release record are currently intact — but the institution that produces it is under documented stress (mass attrition, leadership turnover, proposed reorganization, and a lapsed ICR awaiting renewal for the 2027 cycle). The single most important near-term indicator to monitor is the publication of the 2027 Economic Census 60-day Federal Register notice and ICR reinstatement under OMB Control No. 0607-0998, expected roughly mid-to-late 2026 if the cycle remains on schedule; its absence by early 2027 would warrant escalating Future Data Availability to High Risk.

**Key sources:** Census Bureau 2022 Economic Census release schedule and data tables pages (census.gov); Federal Register 91 FR 56835 ("Current Mandatory Business Surveys," 2026) and 86 FR 48119 / 87 FR 11687 (2022 EC ICR); reginfo.gov ICR 202202-0607-010 and omb.report (0607-0998, expiration 6/30/2025); CRS IF13105 ("Overview of FY2026 Appropriations for the Census Bureau," P.L. 119-74); American Statistical Association, "The Nation's Data at Risk 2025" (Census chapter); AP (May 2025, DOGE/Census surveys); NPR (April 2025, Census brain drain); Government Executive (July 2025, 1,300 staff losses); Bloomberg Law (Oct 2025, RIF notices); The Census Project (Jan 2026, FY2026 minibus).
